# Example support bundle specs

This topic includes example support bundle specifications. For more, see the [Troubleshoot example repository](https://github.com/replicatedhq/troubleshoot/tree/main/examples/support-bundle) in GitHub.

Each example is a self-contained spec. You can copy the collectors and analyzers from an example into your existing spec, or add the example to your release as its own Secret. When a support bundle is generated, all of the specs in the cluster are combined into a single bundle. For more information, see [Combine support bundle specs](/vendor/support-modular-support-bundle-specs).

## Check application health

This example shows how to use the `deploymentStatus` analyzer to check an application's health.
The `deploymentStatus` analyzer uses data from the default `clusterResources` collector to check if liveness probes are passing and if the required number of replicas are ready for an application deployment.

Replicated recommends using the `deploymentStatus` analyzer to check application health because it doesn't require any additional collectors besides `clusterResources`. It also requires no additional RBAC permissions. The `http`, `exec`, and `runPod` collectors can probe health endpoints directly, but each has environment-specific limitations:
- `http` cannot resolve in-cluster DNS from the CLI.
- `exec` requires `pods/exec` RBAC and tools such as `curl`, `wget`, or `nc` in the container.
- `runPod` requires `pods/create` RBAC. In air-gapped environments, the image must already be present on the node.

For more information, see [Deployment Status](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/analyze/deployment-status/) and [Cluster Resources](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/collect/cluster-resources/) in the Troubleshoot documentation.

<DeployStatusSecret/>

## Check HTTP requests

If your application has its own API that serves status, metrics, performance data, and so on, this information can be collected and analyzed.

The example below uses the `http` collector and the `textAnalyze` analyzer to check that an HTTP request to the Slack API at `https://api.slack.com/methods/api.test` made from the cluster returns a successful response of `"status": 200,`.

For more information, see [HTTP](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/collect/http/) and [Regular Expression](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/analyze/regex/) in the Troubleshoot documentation.

<HttpSecret/>

## Collect logs using multiple selectors

The example below uses the `logs` collector to collect logs from various Pods where application workloads are running. It also uses the `textAnalyze` collector to analyze the logs for a known error.

For more information, see [Pod Logs](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/collect/logs/) and [Regular Expression](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/analyze/regex/) in the Troubleshoot documentation.

You can use the `selector` attribute of the `logs` collector to find Pods that have the specified labels. Depending on the complexity of an application's labeling schema, you might need a few different declarations of the logs collector, as shown in this example. You can include the `logs` collector as many times as needed.

<LogsSelectorsSecret/>

## Collect logs using `limits`

The example below uses the `logs` collector to collect Pod logs from the Pod where the application is running. This specification uses the `limits` field to set a `maxAge` and `maxLines` to limit the output provided.

For more information, see [Pod Logs](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/collect/logs/) in the Troubleshoot documentation.

## Collect Prometheus metrics {#prometheus}

If your application runs alongside a Prometheus server, you can include the results of PromQL queries in the support bundle.

The following example uses a `runPod` collector to run `curl` against the Prometheus query API from inside the cluster. The JSON response from Prometheus is saved to `prometheus-up/prometheus-up.log` in the bundle, and the `textAnalyze` analyzer checks that the query succeeded. Update the URL to match the Prometheus service name, namespace, and port in your environment, and add a collector for each query that you want to include. Set `namespace` to a namespace where the support bundle can create Pods, such as your application's namespace. The Pod does not need to run in the same namespace as Prometheus because the URL uses the full service name.

This approach works for every installation method because the request is sent from a Pod in the cluster. It requires `pods/create` RBAC. In air-gapped environments, the `curl` image must be available to the cluster.

For more information, see [Run Pods](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/collect/run-pod/) and [Regular Expression](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/analyze/regex/) in the Troubleshoot documentation.

<PrometheusRunPodSecret/>

### Alternatives to the `runPod` collector

You can also query Prometheus with the `http` collector, but only when the support bundle is generated from inside the cluster, such as from the KOTS Admin Console. The `http` collector sends the request from wherever the support bundle is generated. When a customer runs `kubectl support-bundle` from a workstation, a cluster-internal address such as `http://prometheus-server.monitoring.svc` does not resolve. The bundle is still generated, but the collector output contains a `no such host` error instead of metrics.

If the cluster runs [prometheus-adapter](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prometheus-adapter) or a similar adapter that serves the `custom.metrics.k8s.io` API, you can use the `customMetrics` collector to read metrics through the Kubernetes API without running a Pod. The collector writes each metric to `metrics/<resource kind>/<metric name>/` in the bundle. The metric names that are available depend on the adapter configuration. To list them, run `kubectl get --raw /apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1`. For more information, see [Kubernetes Custom Metrics](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/collect/custom-metrics/) in the Troubleshoot documentation.

```yaml
spec:
  collectors:
    - customMetrics:
        metricRequests:
          - namespace: my-app
            resourceMetricName: pods/kube_pod_container_status_restarts
```

:::note
The `customMetrics` collector is not related to the Replicated SDK custom metrics feature. For information about sending custom metrics to the Vendor Portal, see [Configure custom metrics](/vendor/custom-metrics).
:::

## Run and analyze a pod

The example below uses the `textAnalyze` analyzer to check that a command successfully executes in a Pod running in the cluster. The Pod specification is defined in the `runPod` collector.

For more information, see [Run Pods](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/collect/run-pod/) and [Regular Expression](https://troubleshoot.sh/docs/analyze/regex/) in the Troubleshoot documentation.

<RunPodsSecret/>

### Pass a credential to the pod {#run-pod-credentials}

If a collector needs a credential, such as a database password, use a `runPod` collector and pass the credential to the Pod with `env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef`. The kubelet resolves the credential when the Pod starts, so the credential never appears in the spec.

The following example tests a PostgreSQL connection. The `PGPASSWORD` environment variable is read from the `my-app-postgres` Secret, and the `textAnalyze` analyzer checks the output that the Pod writes to `/postgres-connection.log` in the bundle. The `namespace` field defaults to `default`, so set it to the namespace where the Secret exists.

:::important
The `runPod` collector saves everything that the Pod writes to stdout into the support bundle. Make sure that the command does not print the credential. For example, do not echo the environment variable or run a client with verbose or debug logging enabled.
:::

<RunPodsCredentialsSecret/>

You can use the same pattern in preflight checks, but the Secret must already exist in the cluster when the preflight checks run. For more information, see [Use a credential in a preflight check](/vendor/preflight-defining#credentials) in _Define preflight checks_.
